column2: Leaving behind those masses of arrows, the two lords, surrounded by friends, of incomparable valour, entered their camp happily, like Vasava and Achyuta at a sacrifice.
Honoured with praise for the increase of their victory by gods, gandharvas, men and charanas, great sages, yakshas and great serpents, having slain Karna in the great battle then.
[Krishna said:] "Vritra was slain by the destroyer of Bala, Karna by you, Dhananjaya; people will speak of the slaying of Karna and Vritra together.
Vritra was slain by the thunderbolt-wielder in an equal fight with great splendour; Karna was slain by you with the bow and sharp arrows.
Let us tell this valour of yours, renowned in the world and bringing fame, to the wise king of dharma, son of Kunti.
Having told the king of dharma of Karna's slaying in battle, long desired, you will be free of debt."
Saying "So be it," Partha; Keshava, bull of the Yadus, calmly turned the chariot of that best of chariot-warriors.
Govinda said these words to Dhrishtadyumna, Yudhamanyu, the sons of Madri, Vrikodara and Yuyudhana:
Stand ready facing the enemy, good luck to you, until it is announced to the king that Karna has been slain by Arjuna.
Permitted by those heroes, he went to the king's quarters, and taking Partha with him Govinda saw Yudhishthira.
Krishna, smiling slightly, said to King Yudhishthira, the slayer of foes, with joined palms, Achyuta:

By good fortune the Gandiva-bowman and the Pandava Vrikodara are well, and you too, king, and the two sons of Madri, the Pandavas.
mahabharata:8:69.15	Freed from this destruction, hero, from this hair-raising battle, do quickly the tasks that come next, O lord of the earth.
mahabharata:8:69.16	Vaikartana, cruel, the mighty charioteer's son, is slain; by good fortune you conquer, king of kings, by good fortune you prosper, Pandava.
mahabharata:8:69.17	He who, the lowest of good men, spoke of Krishna won at dice—today the earth drinks the blood of that charioteer's son.
mahabharata:8:69.18	He lies, his limbs torn by arrows, your foe, bull of the Kurus; behold him, tiger among men, pierced in many places by arrows.
Yudhishthira, delighted, honoured the Dasharha, and said with affection, "By good fortune, by good fortune!", king of kings.
This is not marvellous in you, mighty-armed son of Devaki, that Partha, with you as charioteer, should show such manliness today.
Taking Krishna's right arm with its armlet, the best of the Kurus, upholder of dharma, said to both Keshava and Arjuna:

You are the gods Nara and Narayana, told of by Narada, devoted to establishing dharma, ancient best of men.
mahabharata:8:69.23	And Krishna Dvaipayana, the wise lord, told me this divine tale again and again, mighty-armed one.
mahabharata:8:69.24	By your power, Krishna, Dhananjaya with Gandiva conquers the foes facing him and has never turned away anywhere.
mahabharata:8:69.25	Victory is certain for us and no defeat, when you have become Partha's charioteer in the battle.
Having said this, O great king, the great chariot-warrior mounted that gold-adorned chariot yoked with ivory-white horses with black tails,
surrounded by his own force, the tiger among men; and having permitted what was dear to the heroes Krishna and Arjuna,
he came to see the battlefield and the many events there, speaking to the two heroes Madhava and Phalguna.
In the battle he saw Karna, best of men, lying shattered on all sides by arrows loosed from Gandiva.
Seeing Karna slain with his son, King Yudhishthira praised the two tigers among men, Madhava and the Pandava.

Today I am king of the earth, Govinda, with my brothers, protected by you as protector, the hero and wise one.
mahabharata:8:69.32	Seeing the proud Radheya, the tiger among men, slain, that evil-souled son of Dhritarashtra will despair today of life and of kingdom, now that the great chariot-warrior Karna is slain.
mahabharata:8:69.33	By your grace we are fulfilled, best of men, and you and the Gandiva-bowman are victorious, joy of the Yadus; by good fortune you conquer, Govinda, by good fortune Karna is felled.
Thus, many times delighted, King Yudhishthira, the king of dharma, praised Janardana and Arjuna, king of kings.
Then the great chariot-warriors, filled with joy, surrounded by Bhima and all his brothers, congratulated the king.
Nakula, Sahadeva, the Pandava Vrikodara and Satyaki, O great king, the foremost chariot-warrior of the Vrishnis,
Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin, the Pandavas, Panchalas and Srinjayas honoured the son of Kunti when the charioteer's son was slain.
Having congratulated the king, Yudhishthira son of Pandu, those victorious ones who had attained their aim, keen for battle, strikers,
praising the two Krishnas, scorchers of foes, with words of praise, went to their own camp, those great chariot-warriors, filled with joy.
Thus this great, hair-raising destruction came to pass through your ill counsel, O king; why do you grieve over the past?
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing that unwelcome news, King Dhritarashtra fell senseless on the ground, the Kaurava, in utmost pain; so too did the true-vowed goddess Gandhari, who sees dharma.
Vidura and Sanjaya supported the king, comforting both the king and the queen.
Likewise the royal women raised Gandhari; comforted by them both, the king remained silent, his mind blank.
[Sanjaya said:] The Samshaptakas are all slain, the Kambojas with the Shakas, the Mlecchas, mountaineers and Yavanas felled.
The easterners, O great king, and the southerners are slain everywhere; the northerners all slain, and the westerners, O lord of men; kings and princes are slain on every side, O king.
Duryodhana is slain, O king, as the Pandava said; with his thigh broken, O great king, he lies smeared with dust.
Dhrishtadyumna is slain, O king, and Shikhandin the unconquered, Uttamaujas and Yudhamanyu, and the Prabhadrakas, O king.
The Panchalas, tigers among men, and the Chedis are destroyed; all your sons are slain and the sons of Draupadi, O Bharata; Karna's son, the brave and mighty Vrishasena, is slain.
Men are all slain, elephants felled, chariot-warriors, tiger among men, and horses slain in the battle.
A remnant only of the camp has been made, O lord, of yours and of the Pandava heroes, having met one another.
The world, bewildered by time, was left mostly of women; seven remain on the Pandava side and three of Dhritarashtra's.
And those five brothers, Vasudeva and Satyaki, Kripa, Kritavarman and Drona's son, best of victors—
these and you, O great king, these chariot-warriors remain, best of kings, of all the akshauhinis assembled, lord of men; the rest are all gone to death.
The whole world was destroyed by Time, O best of the Bharatas, with Duryodhana put foremost in the enmity, O Bharata.
Hearing this cruel speech, the lord of men Dhritarashtra fell on the ground, O great king, deprived of his senses.
When he had fallen, the greatly renowned Vidura too fell, O great king, wasted by the king's calamity.
Gandhari, best of kings, and all the Kuru women suddenly fell to the ground on hearing that cruel speech.
The royal circle lay fallen senseless on the ground then, and a great lamenting tale was painted as on a cloth.
With difficulty King Dhritarashtra slowly regained his breath, wasted by the calamity of his sons.
Regaining consciousness, the king, trembling, in utmost pain, looking in all directions, said to the minister (Vidura):
Wise Kshatta of great intellect, you are my refuge, best of the Bharatas; I am without protector, utterly bereft of sons. Having said so, he fell senseless again.
Seeing him fallen, whatever kinsmen he had sprinkled him with cold water and fanned him with fans.
After a long time the lord of the earth was comforted, silent, brooding, wasted by the calamity of his sons, sighing like a crooked serpent thrown into a pot, O lord of men.
Sanjaya too wept there, seeing the king afflicted, and all the women and the renowned Gandhari.
Then, after a long time, Dhritarashtra, tiger among men, again and again bewildered, said to Vidura:
Let all the women go, and the renowned Gandhari, and all these friends; my mind is greatly shaken.
Thus addressed, the minister, O best of the Bharatas, trembling again and again, slowly dismissed those women.
Then all those women went out, O best of the Bharatas, and all the friends too, seeing the king afflicted.
Then, seeing the king there come to his senses, scorcher of foes, weeping, greatly afflicted, Sanjaya, dejected,
with joined palms comforted the king as he sighed again and again, and Kshatta with sweet words.
Sighing as if smoking, shaking his hands again and again, and having reflected, O great king, he then spoke these words.

Ah, great sorrow, that I hear from you, charioteer, that the Pandavas are safe and unimpaired in the battle.
mahabharata:9:2.4	Surely my heart is made of thunderbolt-essence and very firm, since it does not burst into a thousand pieces hearing that my sons are slain.
mahabharata:9:2.5	Remembering their words and their childhood play, Sanjaya, my heart is greatly torn today hearing of the slaying of my sons.
mahabharata:9:2.6	Though through blindness I had no sight of their forms, the joy of fatherly affection was ever held for them.
mahabharata:9:2.7	Hearing of them as they passed childhood, stood in youth and reached middle age, I was glad, sinless one.
mahabharata:9:2.8	Hearing today that they are slain, their sovereignty and splendour taken, I find peace nowhere, overwhelmed with anguish for my sons.
mahabharata:9:2.9	Come, come, son, king of kings, to me, now without protector; bereft of you, mighty-armed one, what refuge shall I go to?
mahabharata:9:2.11	That compassion, that affection, that great honour of yours, king—how were you slain by the Parthas, unconquered in battles?
mahabharata:9:2.12	How do you, who enjoyed with the kings assembled, lie slain on the ground like a common, ignoble king?
mahabharata:9:2.13	Who will say to me when I rise in the morning 'Father, father', 'Great king', 'Lord of the world' again and again?
mahabharata:9:2.14	Who will embrace me by the neck with eyes wet with love and say 'Instruct me, Kaurava'? Say those good words to me.
mahabharata:9:2.15	Surely I heard your word, my son: 'This earth is mine more than Partha's.'
mahabharata:9:2.16	Bhagadatta, Kripa, Shalya, the Avanti king and Jayadratha, Bhurishravas, Somadatta, the great king Bahlika,
mahabharata:9:2.17	Ashvatthaman, Bhoja, the mighty Magadha, Brihadbala, the Kashi king, Shakuni son of Subala,
mahabharata:9:2.18	Mlecchas by many thousands, Shakas with Yavanas, Sudakshina, the Kamboja and the lord of the Trigartas,
mahabharata:9:2.19	the Grandsire Bhishma, Bharadvaja's son, Gautama, Shrutayus, Achyutayus and the valiant Shatayus,
mahabharata:9:2.20	Jalasandha, Arshyashringi, the rakshasa Alayudha, the mighty-armed Alambusa and the great chariot-warrior Subahu—
mahabharata:9:2.21	these and many other kings, best of kings, all were ready for my sake to give up life in battle, lord.
mahabharata:9:2.22	Standing in the midst of them, surrounded by my brothers, I shall fight the Parthas and all the Panchalas,
mahabharata:9:2.23	the Chedis, tiger among kings, the sons of Draupadi in battle, Satyaki, Kuntibhoja and the rakshasa Ghatotkacha.
mahabharata:9:2.24	Even one of them, O great king, would be able to hold back the Pandavas as they rush enraged in battle; how much more when the heroes are together, having made enmity with the Pandavas?
mahabharata:9:2.25	Or all of these together with the Pandava's followers will fight, king of kings, and slay them in battle.
mahabharata:9:2.26	Karna alone with me will slay the Pandavas; then the kings, the heroes, will stand under my command.
mahabharata:9:2.27	And their leader, the mighty Vasudeva, does not arm himself, O king—so he told me.
mahabharata:9:2.28	As he spoke thus, charioteer, in my presence many times, I reasonably saw the Pandavas slain in battle.
mahabharata:9:2.29	Where my sons are slain standing among them and striving in battle, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.30	Where Bhishma, the mighty lord of the world, was slain, meeting Shikhandin like a lion a jackal,
mahabharata:9:2.31	and Drona the Brahmana, master of all weapons, was slain by the Pandavas in battle, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.32	Where Bhurishravas and Somadatta were slain in battle, and Bahlika, O great king, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.33	Where Sudakshina and the Kaurava Jalasandha were slain, and Shrutayus and Achyutayus, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.34	Where Brihadbala was slain, and the mighty Magadha, the Avanti king and the lord of the Trigartas, and many Samshaptakas, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.35	Alambusa, O king, and the rakshasa Alayudha, and Arshyashringi were slain, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.36	Where the Narayanas were slain and the Gopalas arrogant in battle, and Mlecchas by many thousands, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.37	Where Shakuni son of Subala and the mighty Kaitavya were slain with their forces, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.38	Where kings and princes, heroes with arms like iron clubs, were slain in great numbers, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.39	Where kshatriyas gathered from many countries, Sanjaya, were all slain in battle, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.40	And my sons and mighty grandsons, friends and brothers were slain, what is that but fate?
mahabharata:9:2.41	A man is surely born joined to fortune; he who is joined to fortune obtains good.
mahabharata:9:2.42	Bereft of my fortune and of my sons here, Sanjaya, how shall I be now, old, fallen into the power of my foes?
mahabharata:9:2.43	I see nothing else here, lord, other than living in the forest; I shall go to the forest, without kinsmen, with my relatives destroyed.
mahabharata:9:2.44	Nothing else is good for me, Sanjaya, except going to the forest, now that I have come to this state, like a bird with clipped wings.
mahabharata:9:2.45	Where Duryodhana is slain, Shalya slain in battle, Duhshasana killed and the mighty Vikarna,
mahabharata:9:2.46	how shall I hear the supreme sound of Bhimasena, by whom alone my hundred sons were slain in the battle?
mahabharata:9:2.47	As he speaks again and again of Duryodhana's slaying, scorched by grief and sorrow, I shall not be able to hear his harsh words.
Thus the king, scorched by grief, his kinsmen slain, bewildered again and again, overwhelmed with anguish for his sons,
lamenting a long time, Dhritarashtra, son of Ambika, sighing long and hot and brooding on the defeat,
the king, tormented by great sorrow, O best of the Bharatas, again questioned Gavalgana's son, the charioteer, truthfully:

Hearing that Bhishma and Drona were slain and the charioteer's son felled, what did my men do for a commander, a leader?
mahabharata:9:2.52	Whichever leader my men appoint in the battle, the Pandavas kill him in very short time.
mahabharata:9:2.53	Bhishma was slain at the head of the battle by Kiritin in your sight; so too Drona was slain in the sight of all.
mahabharata:9:2.54	So too the glorious charioteer's son Karna was slain by Kiritin in the sight of all the kings and of you.
mahabharata:9:2.55	Long ago I was told by the great-souled Vidura that through Duryodhana's offence the people would perish.
mahabharata:9:2.56	Some do not see rightly, being foolish, others see rightly; that was my foolish word.
mahabharata:9:2.57	What the righteous, far-seeing Vidura told me, the word of the truthful one has come true.
mahabharata:9:2.58	Tell me again, Gavalgani, the fruit of the wrong I formerly did with a mind struck by fate.
mahabharata:9:2.59	Who was at the head of the divisions when Karna was felled, and what chariot-warrior went against Arjuna and Vasudeva?
mahabharata:9:2.60	Who guarded the right wheel of the king of the Madras in the battle, who the left, of him who wished to fight, and who was behind the hero?
mahabharata:9:2.61	How was the mighty king of the Madras slain in the battle by the Pandavas while you were assembled, or my son, Sanjaya?
mahabharata:9:2.62	Tell all as it truly was of the great destruction of the Bharatas, and how my son Duryodhana was slain in the battle.
mahabharata:9:2.63	How all the Panchalas were slain with their followers, Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin and the five sons of Draupadi,
mahabharata:9:2.64	how the Pandavas escaped, and the two Satvatas in the battle, and Kripa, Kritavarman and Bharadvaja's son,
mahabharata:9:2.65	how and of what kind the battle took place and what has now happened—I wish to hear it all, for you are skilled, Sanjaya.
[Sanjaya said:] When the charioteer's son was slain by the great-souled Pandava and the armies fled and were repeatedly gathered,
when your son was turned away, his mind struck by grief, and the armies greatly agitated, having seen Partha's prowess,
when the armies brooded, afflicted by sorrow, O Bharata, hearing the great roar of the troops being crushed,
seeing the marks of kings deformed in battle, fallen chariot-seats and chariots of the great-souled,
seeing elephants and foot-soldiers slain in the battle, O revered one, and the battlefield most dreadful, like Rudra's playground,
and the hundreds of thousands of kings gone into oblivion, Kripa, filled with compassion, endowed with age and character,
the glorious one, went to the king and said, out of anger, being unable to hold back his speech, to Duryodhana:

Duryodhana, hear what I shall say to you, Kaurava; hearing it, do it, great king, if it pleases you, sinless one.
mahabharata:9:3.10	There is no better path, king of kings, than the duty of war, relying on which kshatriyas fight, bull of kshatriyas.

[The hunter said:] "Having slain Vritra, the king of the gods obtained the best share; having destroyed the sacrifice, the trident-bearer god got a share; do the god's act, quickly kill the serpent, let there be no doubt."
It is fitting that a kshatriya with fame attains heaven without doubt; for not one of the brave is slain here facing away.
